claims.text: The starting material is an equiatomic Ti–Hf–V–Zr–Nb alloy, corresponding to approximately 20 at.% of each element.
The starting Ti–Hf–V–Zr–Nb alloy is a solid-solution high-entropy alloy.
The starting alloy has a measurable baseline superconducting transition temperature and superconducting gap.
Part of the V can be replaced by Nb while retaining at least 5 at.% of every constituent element.
Replacing V with Nb increases the alloy's average valence electron count.
The relative d-electron contributions of Nb and V modulate the local electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Increasing Nb at the expense of V raises the density of states near the Fermi level.
A higher density of states near the Fermi level strengthens electron–phonon coupling.
Stronger electron–phonon coupling increases the superconducting transition temperature.
Stronger electron–phonon coupling increases the superconducting gap.
A moderate increase in Nb with a corresponding decrease in V will produce a higher Tc than the equiatomic baseline.
A moderate increase in Nb with a corresponding decrease in V will produce a larger superconducting gap than the equiatomic baseline.
A clear composition–Tc correlation will occur before secondary phases or significant disorder develop.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains a homogeneous solid solution and every element remains at or above 5 at.%.
Secondary-phase formation or significant changes in lattice disorder can confound the relationship between Nb/V ratio and superconductivity.
Minor local disorder or unintended phase segregation may affect superconducting properties independently of the intended electron-count change.
The proposed samples are to be arc melted and homogenized at 1000°C for 24 hours under an inert atmosphere.
Failure of increasing Nb content to produce a monotonic or statistically significant increase in both Tc and superconducting gap would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Phase segregation is defined as outside the mechanism's applicable boundary and as a confounder, but an enhancement attributable to phase segregation is also described as falsifying the mechanism. Under the stated boundary, such a result would ordinarily make the experiment inconclusive rather than directly falsify the hypothesis.
